q: 1. A plate load test is useful to estimate
options: Both bearing capacity and settlement of foundation
explain: The plate load test provides a load-settlement curve from which both the safe bearing capacity and the expected settlement of the actual foundation can be estimated.

q: 2. A shallow foundation is defined as a foundation which
options: Has a depth of embedment less than its width
Is resting on the ground surface
explain: By Terzaghi's definition, a foundation is 'shallow' when its depth of embedment (Df) is less than or approximately equal to its width (B), typically Df ≤ B.

q: 3. The depth upto which the stress increment due to the applied loads can produce significant settlement is called as .............
explain: Significant depth is the term for the zone below a foundation where applied stress increments meaningfully contribute to settlement.

q: 4. The minimum depth of exploration in case of gravity dam is .............
explain: For gravity dams, exploration typically extends to a depth roughly equal to the height of the dam to characterize the stressed foundation zone.

q: 5. Stress distribution on the failure plane in the case of a triaxial test is .............
explain: In a properly conducted triaxial test, stresses are applied uniformly across the specimen's cross-section and failure plane.

q: 6. In unconfined compression test, around stress is .............
explain: The unconfined compression test applies no lateral (confining/cell) pressure, so the minor principal stress is zero.

q: 7. The expression for critical gradient is .............
explain: Critical hydraulic gradient is derived by equating upward seepage force to submerged weight: ic = (G-1)/(1+e).

q: 8. Graphical method for the determination of earth pressure
explain: Culmann's graphical method is a well-known trial-wedge construction technique for determining active/passive earth pressure, especially for irregular backfill conditions.

q: 9. The presence of entrapped air in a soil will .............
explain: Entrapped air bubbles block pore channels, reducing the effective flow path and thus decreasing permeability.

q: 10. According to IS code the soil having coefficient of permeability between 104 cm/sec. and 10-2 cm/sec. is termed as
explain: IS classification places soils with permeability in this intermediate range (between highly pervious and impervious) into the semi-pervious category.

q: 11. The value of coefficient of permeability of clays is .............
explain: Clays, with their very fine pores, have extremely low permeability, typically less than 10^-6 cm/s.

q: 12. The angle that Coulomb's failure envelope makes with the horizontal is called
explain: In a Mohr-Coulomb shear strength plot, the slope of the failure envelope line with the horizontal (normal stress) axis is the angle of internal friction, φ.

q: 13. Soils with a value for coefficient of permeability ranging between 10^-4 to 10^-6 are classified as .............
explain: This intermediate permeability range (10^-4 to 10^-6 cm/s) defines semi-pervious soils, such as silts.

q: 14. If the shearing stress is zero on two planes, then the angle between the two planes is
explain: Zero shear stress occurs only on the principal planes, and the two principal planes (major and minor) are always oriented at 90° to each other.

q: 15. Rankin's theory of earth pressure assumes that, back of the wall is
explain: Rankine's theory assumes the back face of the retaining wall is vertical and perfectly smooth (frictionless), simplifying the stress analysis to principal stress conditions.

17. Coefficient of earth pressure at rest is
options: Less than active earth pressure but greater than passive earth pressure
Greater than active earth pressure but less than passive earth pressure
Greater than both the active earth pressure and passive earth pressure
Less than both the active and passive earth pressure
explain: Since Ka < K0 < Kp always (no wall movement gives an intermediate at-rest state between the minimum active and maximum passive states), K0 is greater than Ka but less than Kp.

q: 18. A comparatively sudden reduction in volume of a soil mass under an applied load (due principally to expulsion and compression of gas in the soil voids preceding primary consolidation) is called
explain: This rapid initial volume reduction, occurring due to compression/expulsion of air before true primary consolidation begins, is termed initial consolidation.

q: 19. The type of settlement which causes more trouble for the stability of structure is .............
explain: Differential (uneven) settlement causes structural distortion and cracking, making it far more damaging than uniform settlement.

q: 20. The angle between the abscissa and the tangent to the curve representing the relationship of shearing resistance to normal stress acting within a soil is called
explain: The slope of the shear stress vs normal stress curve (Mohr-Coulomb envelope) with the horizontal axis is, by definition, the angle of internal friction.

q: 21. Consolidation is a process involving
explain: Consolidation is a slow, time-dependent process in which excess pore water pressure dissipates and water is gradually squeezed out of a saturated soil under sustained load.

q: 22. Rise in water table upto the ground surface results in .............
options: reduction of pore water pressure but no change in total stress
increase of pore water pressure and increase in total stress
increase of pore water pressure and increase in total stress
increase of pore water pressure and decrease in total stress
explain: As water table rises, both total stress (due to submerged unit weight change) and pore pressure increase together.

q: 23. The constant of proportionality between seepage velocity and hydraulic gradient is called .............
explain: Seepage (percolation) velocity relates to hydraulic gradient through the coefficient of percolation, which uses the net (void) cross-sectional area.

q: 24. Capillary force is dependent on .............
explain: Capillary rise and force in soil pores are governed primarily by the surface tension of water acting at the air-water meniscus.

q: 25. An isobar is
options: Point below ground surface where net pressure is zero
A curve or contour connecting all points below ground surface of equal vertical stress
A curve or contour connecting all points below ground surface of equal horizontal stress
A location where vertical stress is equal to horizontal stress
explain: An isobar (pressure bulb contour) in soil mechanics connects points of equal vertical stress increase caused by a surface load, used to visualize the pressure bulb beneath a footing.

q: 26. The zone of soil mass above the water table which is saturated by capillary moisture is called .............
explain: The capillary fringe is the zone directly above the water table kept saturated by capillary action.

q: 27. For calculating stress distribution in soils, Boussinesq assumed point load to be
explain: Boussinesq's classical elastic theory for stress distribution assumes a concentrated point load applied at the ground surface (ground level) of a semi-infinite, homogeneous, isotropic elastic medium.

q: 28. The number of heads that are used for defining the water head at a point in a soil mass are .............
explain: Total head at a point is composed of three components: elevation head, pressure head, and velocity head.

q: 29. Velocity head in soils will be .............
explain: Seepage velocities in soil are extremely small, making the velocity head component negligible compared to elevation and pressure heads.

q: 30. The pore water pressure in the capillary zone is .............
explain: Water held in the capillary fringe above the water table is under suction (tension), giving it negative pore water pressure.

q: 31. Hydraulic gradient provided at the downstream side of a hydraulic structures such as dam is called
explain: The hydraulic gradient at the point where seepage water exits the ground on the downstream side of a dam/structure is called the exit gradient, critical for piping/uplift checks.

q: 32. Water which the soil particles freely adsorb from atmosphere by the physical forces of attraction, and is held by the force of adhesion is known as .............
explain: Water adsorbed onto particle surfaces via physical attraction and adhesion can be described by any of these overlapping terms, so all apply.

q: 33. Units of co-efficient of permeability
explain: Coefficient of permeability k has units of velocity (length/time), commonly expressed as cm/sec, since it represents flow velocity under unit hydraulic gradient.

q: 34. Capillary water is held in the interstices of soil due to capillarity forces. The capillary force depends upon .............
explain: Capillary force depends jointly on surface tension, water pressure, and the size of soil pores (which sets the meniscus curvature).

q: 35. Falling head permeability test is preferable when soil sample is
explain: The falling head test suits fine-grained soils (clays) with low permeability, where the small, slow water flow can be accurately measured by the falling head in a standpipe, unlike the constant head test used for sandy soils.

q: 36. Quick sand is
options: A condition in which cohesion is decreased quickly
A sand which can be compacted quickly
A condition in which a cohesionless soil loses its strength because of upward flow of water
explain: Quicksand is not a soil type but a hydraulic condition: upward seepage pressure equals or exceeds the submerged unit weight of a cohesionless soil, reducing effective stress and shear strength to near zero.

q: 37. A soil which does not permit the passage or seepage of any permeant through its voids, is known as .............
explain: A soil that blocks all seepage flow through its voids is, by definition, an impermeable soil.

q: 38. Maximum failures of earth dams are due to
options: Erosion of soil due to flowing water
Leakage through cavities or holes formed by animals
explain: Historically, the most common cause of earth dam failure is erosion/piping of soil caused by uncontrolled seepage/overtopping flowing water eroding the embankment.

q: 39. In most of the practical flow problems in soil mechanics, the flow is .............
explain: Given the very low seepage velocities in soils, flow is almost always laminar, satisfying the basis for Darcy's law.

q: 40. In a flow net
options: Flow lines and equipotential lines meet at right angles to one another
Quantity of water flowing through each flow channel is different
Larger the dimensions of the field, smaller will be the hydraulic gradient
Different potential drop occurs between two successive equipotential lines
explain: A defining property of a properly constructed flow net is that flow lines and equipotential lines always intersect orthogonally (at right angles), forming curvilinear squares.

q: 41. Consolidation theory was due to
explain: Karl Terzaghi formulated the classical one-dimensional theory of consolidation, a cornerstone of modern soil mechanics.

q: 42. Sheet piles are held in position by
options: Adjusting water level on one side
explain: Anchored sheet pile walls are stabilized primarily through tie rods connected to anchors set back in stable ground, in addition to embedment, but tie rods are the key holding mechanism cited here.

q: 43. Consolidation is a process involving
explain: Consolidation is defined by the slow, time-dependent, gradual expulsion of pore water from saturated soil under sustained load, not sudden or abnormal effects.

q: 44. Factor of safety of embankments shall be
explain: For slope stability of embankments against shear failure, a factor of safety of at least 2.5 (or similar high value per this reference) is typically recommended for safety.

q: 45. A critical hydraulic gradient occurs when .............
options: seepage pressure is in upward direction
explain: Critical gradient conditions require upward flow, upward seepage pressure equal to submerged weight, and consequently zero effective stress — all together.

q: 46. The maximum size of plate for plate load test is
explain: As per standard plate load test procedure, the test plate size typically ranges up to about 60 cm (square/circular), used to simulate the foundation's bearing behaviour.

q: 47. Geostatic stresses are due to .............
explain: Geostatic (overburden) stresses arise from the self-weight of the soil mass above a given point.

q: 48. Expansion of soils under shear is known as .............
explain: Dilatancy is the tendency of dense granular soils to expand in volume when subjected to shear.

q: 49. Shearing strength of a cohesionless soil depends upon
explain: For a purely frictional cohesionless soil, shear strength (s = σ tanφ) is fundamentally governed by the normal stress on the failure plane.

q: 50. The stress that is responsible for the mobilization of shearing strength of a soil .............
explain: Shear strength is governed by effective stress (per Terzaghi's principle), not total or pore water pressure alone.
